headline: Rent stabilization ordinance for mobile home parks receives first passage, regulating lot rent increases.
summary: The ordinance changes three chapters of the city code and sets up a Rent Stabilization Board for mobile home parks. A rent cap is tied to 0.34 of the HUD fair market rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the Lewiston-Auburn MSA. A set of wording corrections passed 7-0, and the public hearing was continued to the next regularly scheduled meeting. Two special elections were also ordered: one for six Charter Commission members on April 13th, 2027, and one for the vacant Ward 3 seat.
decisions: Approved 7-0 a set of wording and clarifying corrections to the mobile home park rent ordinance.
Approved first passage 7-0 of the mobile home park lot rent ordinance.
Approved a special election on April 13th, 2027 to elect six Charter Commission members, by a vote of 6-1.
Approved a special election to fill the vacant Ward 3 council seat, by a vote of 5-2.
discussion: Rent Stabilization Board membership: Discussion centered on whether to exclude mobile home residents as well as park owners and their agents. Views favored excluding both groups or including both, to keep the board small and impartial.

Fair market rent and cap: Members proposed defining fair market rent as the HUD two-bedroom rate for the Lewiston-Auburn MSA, which the clerk said could be added at second reading. One member asked whether others would support lowering the 34% figure to 28%.

Campaign contributions and recusal: A member asked whether a councilor who took thousands of dollars from park owners should recuse from the vote. Others said the contributions were disclosed, and that state law does not treat campaign contributions as a thing of value.

Public comment on the ordinance: Speakers urged passage and said the capital improvement and fee language is not a concern. One speaker asked for an independent social and economic impact analysis, and access to the underlying data, before final adoption.

Ward 3 election timing: Discussion focused on holding the election sooner so Ward 3 gets representation earlier. Staff estimated a ward-only election would cost several thousand dollars, and a speaker said Ward 3 would go four months without representation.
